task.title: Study Forensics: Houseplants and depression scores (synthetic)
task.prompt: A cross-sectional survey of 5,000 remote workers asked participants how many houseplants they owned and assessed their depressive symptoms with a standard questionnaire. Those with five or more houseplants reported average depression scores 30 percent lower than those with no plants. The article concludes that "bringing the outdoors in" can improve mental health and urges employers to reimburse plant purchases for home offices. No experimental design is used, and the survey authors acknowledge that plant owners also tended to have higher incomes, more natural light and more leisure time.
task.context:
The synthetic summary equates owning multiple houseplants with improved mental health
based on a cross-sectional survey, ignoring socioeconomic confounders.
task.reference_solution: The synthetic summary equates owning multiple houseplants with improved mental health based on a cross-sectional survey, ignoring socioeconomic confounders. The recommendation for employers to subsidise plants is unsupported by causal evidence.

functional_descriptions: no causal inference is possible from a cross-sectional design
the observed association may be driven by confounding variables
the article makes causal claims from correlational data

common_errors: accepting the causal claim at face value
treating the policy recommendation as evidence-based
task.diagnostic_focus: Can the agent identify correlation-as-causation and confounder blindness?
